title: Architecture and tools
thesis: A roguelike's engineering problem is breadth: hundreds of pieces of content that all want to interact, each tempted to become a special case. The talks converge on the same answers: put content in data run by one interpreter, express behaviour as decoupled actions or events, isolate a deterministic, serializable simulation from its presentation, and buy saves, replays, networking, modding and testing almost for free. Around that core, invest in fast tools and in visibility, because iteration speed and the ability to see inside a generated world decide how good the game gets.

sections.heading: Why roguelike code rots: breadth, special cases and coupling
sections.brief: Open with the diagnosis that frames the whole chapter: a roguelike's hard problem is not per-entity complexity but sheer breadth of interacting content (Nystrom), and every piece of content wants a special case (Compton). Show the convergent failure modes: Compton's giant chain of if statements multiplying with content, Moromisato's weapon-by-creature interaction matrix, Danny Day's inheritance prototype where the god system spread checks through the hierarchy and slowed releases from weekly to every two months, Cronin's reentrant manager spaghetti and Unity-encouraged callback spaghetti in Monster Train, and the cost of legacy and portability code in ADOM and NetHack. Then present the counter-moves the talks share: decouple behaviours so complexity grows linearly rather than quadratically (Nystrom), reify verbs into objects, design each system in isolation with plug points (Blaseball), reuse an existing system when a new feature fits its definition (Improbable's quest-like objects), and leave uniform hooks for the future (NetHack's shield equip function). Stage the tension with Compton's own admission that her specification-driven parser was overengineered and Hinenzon's chore queue whose responsibility drifted: abstraction is not free. End with guidance on when to stop and introduce structure, and why the payoff (Cronin: determinism, saves, replays, undo, previews, tests) justifies it.

sections.heading: Content as data: rules in the engine, things in files
sections.brief: Argue the most convergent position in the chapter: author content as data interpreted by one well-tested engine rather than as code. Lead with Compton's 'don't whittle your own screws' and Biskup's Ultimate ADOM core-rules-engine-plus-external-configuration, then show the same move across many games: Caves of Qud's XML inheritance tree, Cataclysm's JSON nouns and verbs, Hades' traits as numeric modifiers in JSON, Backpack Hero's refactor to inspector-configured trigger/effect/value/target items, Spry Fox's YAML with includes, Angband/Sil-Q's text files, Pagnutti's enemy state machine as two tables, Bioloom's flattened genome, and Yarn Spinner's node-group pools and rules. Gather the benefits the talks name (copy-paste, linting, safe execution of strangers' content, non-programmer authoring, external tools that can index the whole game, future generators per Berman). Set against them the limits: Cronin's Monster Train card-effect scripts broke down on dependent, scaling effects; Hinenzon found narrative timing buried in C# floats; and Biskup deliberately fixes a middle layer of core rules rather than making everything data. End with practical guidance: what belongs in data, what stays in code, and how to give data an escape hatch (Qud's C# parts).

sections.heading: Modelling entities: ECS, components and the alternatives
sections.brief: Stage the chapter's clearest debate. Explain where entity component systems came from (Nystrom: AAA domain splitting and cache-friendly arrays), then set Nystrom's warning that domain-split ECS is a poor fit for turn-based tile roguelikes against Biskup's enthusiastic, modified ECS for Ultimate ADOM (entities as data containers, components with simple behaviour, systems for complex reusable logic, fixed core rules). Show what components buy: soul-swapping by moving the UI-control component, a possessed body becoming an item where ADOM 2's inheritance hierarchies made that hard, slots for swapping material, ten-line amputation built from shared systems, 'emits fire' attachable to anything (Wilson). Present Nystrom's lighter alternatives side by side: capability objects for items and the type object ('breed') pattern, which Biskup's entity templates and flyweight sharing parallel. Close with the costs: weird emergent bugs (a severed spider part granting web spinning), runtime type changes, and practical advice on choosing granularity; NetHack's body-part mapping is a small example of data-driven polymorphism.

sections.heading: Turns, actions and events: where behaviour lives
sections.brief: Cover how a turn is executed and where gameplay logic sits. Start with the two strongest models: Nystrom's command pattern (each turn an Action object, driven by an energy-based speed loop, keeping actors as data) and Danny Day's Desktop Dungeons dynamic event handlers (objects only hold state; handlers listen, change state and emit further events, added and removed at runtime). Show the convergence with Cronin's serializable world commands that never call other commands and with Biskup's event-driven movement phases and event routing. Then lay out the costs and fixes: deterministic handler priority and splitting handlers to break loops, a verbose-events debug mode to recover readability, Day's warning that event systems are cache-unfriendly (fine for turn-based, not real-time), and Hades' modifier-ordering bug. Add the alternatives and variants: coroutines that mirror the game's call stack (Berman) versus Cronin's view that coroutines tangle concerns, one controller for players and monsters alike (Bloomquist), priority queues for blocking events (Sunshine Shuffle), finite state machines, Spirit of the Ages' single concern mechanism, ritual interpreters and indexed procedural triggers. End with a decision guide: actions vs events vs coroutines.

sections.heading: Isolate the simulation: state, logic and presentation
sections.brief: Make the case for a 'black box' simulation, the architecture several talks independently arrive at. Lead with Cronin's principle of strict separation of static data, mutable state, logic and presentation, and his Monster Train world-engine design where commands modify an isolated state and presentation subscribes to emitted state changes; set beside it Biskup's lament that ADOM's UI runs through all the code, making a mobile version practically impossible, and Ultimate ADOM's answer (engine on its own thread sending minimal UI signals). Show converging techniques: one serializable world state of integers including the RNG, one-way top-down control, presentation learning about the world only through state-change records, Desktop Dungeons giving UI handlers lowest priority, game state as pure functions for tree search (Kingsford), arena-allocated state that can be copied and sent (Berman). Then the payoffs: headless servers without Unity (Inkbound), previews that need determinism designed in from the start, mid-battle saves and run verification Monster Train never got. End with how to retrofit the separation and how to debug a coupled codebase meanwhile (categorized logging).

sections.heading: Presenting a turn-based world: animation, timing and text
sections.brief: Treat the presentation layer that sits on top of the simulation. Begin with Cronin's point that the black box has no concept of time, so presentation sequences animations from emitted changes after the sim has finished, and set it against Jeremiah Reid's admission that synchronising animations with the logical order of simultaneous events (an arrow landing before its target moves) is the hardest part of juice, still glitchy in Golden Krone Hotel. Then the techniques: delta-time animation with a global time multiplier to 'lie about time', Thomas Robertson's effect atoms with blocking and concurrent lists, a fixed 60 fps timer for terminal Tetris, smart variables that draw themselves for prototypes. The second half covers text as presentation: NetHack's 'You' function and body-part mapping, Monster Train card text bound to effect values, and Caves of Qud's localization rebuild (typed template replacers, gettext-style _S/_T calls with translator context, Roslyn-based string extraction, and the missing in-context authoring tools). End with guidance on keeping presentation one-way and text generated from data.

sections.heading: Saves, determinism, replays and networking
sections.brief: Argue that saving, replaying and networking are one problem: can the game's state and its changes be serialized and replayed deterministically? Lead with Danny Day's event-string save games that let content be removed without ever resetting players' progress, Cronin's save/replay/network-by-commands, Greg L's one-bit-per-destructible-object saves on top of a regenerated seed (with Star Trek 1971's lossy quadrant storage and Anderson's compressed sand as relatives), and the warning from NetHack that changing a struct breaks every save and bones file (plus one attempt to fix that with JSON introspection). Then networking as a spectrum: Zeyfang's NecroDancer rollback netcode (snapshot every tick, beat-keyed then time-derived turn IDs, client-authoritative beat judgement) versus Plummer's two wasted months on rollback before realising a turn-based game only needed deterministic lockstep, with Anderson's 'network inputs, not state' for falling sand. Include replay as verification (Liotta's server replaying keypresses to stop cheating, code shared client and server), replays as explanation (Crawl's ttyrecs), seeds built for debugging that became contests (Brogue), and lighter models (polled REST for Twitch). End with guidance on choosing the cheapest model that works.

sections.heading: Designing for modders
sections.brief: Build on the data-driven section to cover modding as an architectural goal. Lead with the convergent advice to plan for modding from the start because retrofitting is harder (Moromisato, citing Caves of Qud and Dwarf Fortress; Ritchie's Axu, built so modders have the developer's tools). Contrast the traditional model (forking the source, as NetHack variants did) with data overlays and scripting hooks: Moromisato's onAttack/onDefend events let independent mods combine without coordinating. Then the costs: hook points multiply, mods find every engine bug, and Ray's Caves of Qud examples show both how component granularity can block modders (rocket boots) and the power-versus-comprehensibility tension as data becomes a programming language; Peglin's Unity components were fast for the team but not easy for modders. End with Moromisato's practical rules (dogfood your mod system for first-party content, require an API version from day one, generate mod docs from the registering code) and Pipkin's view of the browser's view-source as permission to touch.

sections.heading: Little languages: writing rules in a language built for them
sections.brief: Argue that the format your content and rules are written in is a programming language whether you meant it or not (Compton), and that choosing or designing one deliberately lets you spend effort on the design problem rather than incidental chores (Kovach). Present the concrete families: Kovach's relational rule systems (world state as typed facts, logic rules as abstraction, traceability of every fact, PuzzleScript's one-rule Sokoban, Inform 7's near-English), Seth Cooper's TRBT tile-rewrite rules driven by behaviour trees with hidden layers and no object identity, Cronin's proposed action graph for card effects, and Reed's call for writer-friendly DSLs. Then Compton's design principles for 'polite' languages: ecosystems not syntax, informal properties, scaffolding, structure editors, unfoldable syntax, safe embedding, separating engine from tools (Tracery/Cheap Bots Done Quick versus the over-bundled Chancery). Close with declarative tools you already have: spreadsheets as a game runtime (Tyler Robertson's iterative-calculation tricks) and SQL recursive CTEs to enumerate enemy move traces (Pagnutti), plus OpenSCAD's limits. Set Kovach's 'language as conduct' framing against the cost of learning a new paradigm (Cooper's user study).

sections.heading: Tools that keep designers iterating
sections.brief: Argue that tool value is measured in turnaround: JP LeBreton's liveness (tight loops, visible hidden state, no compile-reboot-reload) and Leigh Alexander's near-zero-latency spreadsheets that update a running instance converge on the same rule. Show the techniques: hot reloading by sharing data between editor and game, finding the operations done several times a minute and cutting their cost, Liotta's instant edit/play level editor, McCormick's console-logged objects for live balancing, and Spry Fox's design dashboard derived from configs (sortable views, open-in-editor, 'dropped by' loot inspection, calendar coverage) as a single source of truth replacing desynced spreadsheets. Then procgen tooling: Egart's modular, parameterised generator steps in a node graph and his point that friendliness is the secretly hard part; Pepers on wrapping generation in sliders; Hidden Door's pipeline of small composable tasks around an LLM for interpretability; generator inspectors (Tea Garden), MCTS level tools in Godot, Twine-to-audio pipelines. Add LeBreton's 'build a more powerful editor and export down' and REXPaint as a shared roguelike tool, with Nifflas' caution that internal tools need real UX work before release.

sections.heading: Catching problems before players do: validation and automated play
sections.brief: Cover automated checking of data and of the game itself. Lead with Horneman's static cross-referencing of level data against the room list in CI, his principle that validation matters most where independently authored assets meet, and his cautionary tale that proving a location-reservation system never runs dry was far harder than it sounded. Converge it with Spry Fox's DarkConfig validators, Jeremy Rose's schema generated from TypeScript types and run on every Cataclysm release, Caves of Qud's replacer examples that double as unit tests and docs, and NetHack's level compiler catching errors at compile time. Then automated play: Neo Cab ran its actual ink game headlessly thousands of times (Phenry Ewing), Kingsford's MCTS playtester and fuzzer with generic rewards, set against his warnings that it plays optimally, not like a human, and needs a fast compiled loop. Add Withington's testable generators that output minimal encodings, and the counterexample of The Hobbit's unverifiable emergent simulation plus NetHack's defensive coding. End with what to automate first.

sections.heading: Seeing inside a running game: debugging, logging and telemetry
sections.brief: Argue that a procedural game has no static scene to inspect, so visibility must be built (Birke: an extensible debug menu early). Lead with the convergence on recording everything: Horneman's point that individually fine dynamic selections can add up to a bad experience visible only through analytics, Crawl's machine-readable milestones queryable by an IRC bot (Alan Malloy), the Blaseball archivists' rule to record raw data because tomorrow's story is in it, and NAO's 200 GB of ttyrecs. Then public servers as debugging infrastructure: Crawl posting every crash with morgue, trace and save to the dev channel and auto-updating trunk, NAO surfacing rare bugs, and the security and hosting choices Drew Streib describes for dgamelaunch. Close with code legibility as a debugging tool (NetHack's plain-English comments and ASCII diagrams) and DCSS's AAA-scale investment in player-facing infrastructure.

sections.heading: Choosing a foundation: languages, engines and libraries
sections.brief: A short, practical section. Lead with JP LeBreton's argument that building your own engine or tool is about putting your values into practice, set against Biskup choosing Unity for Ultimate ADOM's multi-platform plans after painful hand-written ports. Then the beginner's view: Josh Ge says language matters little (use what you know, Python if fresh) and libtcod does the roguelike heavy lifting; Daigle's GameMaker 'sweet spot' (and his note that he'd pick Godot now); the browser as a runtime (McCormick, with rot.js) and JavaScript for shared client-server code; SquidLib for Java; LeBreton on engines imposing as few speed restrictions as possible. Include history for perspective: curses made Rogue possible, early ADOM's 'neolithic' tooling, and no-code bot hosting. End with a short decision list.

sections.heading: Performance and hard constraints
sections.brief: Close with the edge cases: where performance actually bites a roguelike and what tight constraints teach. Most turn-based roguelikes do not have cache-miss problems (see the ECS section), so lead with the places they do: quadratic perception in ecosystem sims (Bioloom at about 50 creatures), cellular automata where memory layout (Morton order), block parallelism and skipping unchanged chunks matter (Scott Anderson, Noita), a CA-based persistent world (Nematode), Ultimate ADOM's million-entity prototype and its surprising Java-versus-C# gap, Forska's per-click time budget, rooms to bound simulation scope. Include Albert Ford's field-of-view comparison as a case of trading efficiency against correctness (raycasting oversamples; shadowcasting with beveled walls and centre checks is efficient, consistent and symmetric), and 3D asset budgets (LOD, texture packing, instancing, mesh combining). Then constraints as craft: Greg L's bit-level thinking (bitfields, wraparound, fixed point, fast inverse square root), Hack's separate generator binary on the PDP-11, NetHack's Amiga overlays, Alphaman on a floppy, PICO-8's token limit and Uxn's freeing 64KB.
